summary.text: Stellar evolution is the process by which a star changes over time, and a star's mass decides its path and how long it lives.
Stars form from collapsing clouds of gas and dust, settle into the main sequence, and are powered by nuclear fusion for most of their existence.
Most changes are too slow to see, so astrophysicists study many stars at different points in their lives and simulate them with computer models.

items.prompt: Why can't astronomers learn how stars age by watching one star from birth to death?

options.label: Stars cannot be seen through a telescope
Every star ends its life in one night
Only the Sun can be studied closely
Most changes are too slow to detect, even over centuries

items.explain: Most stellar changes happen too slowly to see, so astrophysicists observe many stars at different points in their lives and use computer models.

items.prompt: A small, cold red dwarf and a massive, hot O-type star both begin burning hydrogen today. Which stays on the main sequence longer?

options.label: The massive O-type star, since it holds more fuel
The red dwarf, by a huge margin
They stay for about the same time
Neither, because both leave right away

items.explain: Red dwarfs fuse hydrogen slowly and last hundreds of billions of years or more, while massive O-type stars leave the main sequence after a few million years.

items.prompt: A star like the Sun has finally used up its nuclear fuel. What becomes of it?

options.label: Its core becomes a dense white dwarf and its outer layers drift away as a planetary nebula
It explodes as a supernova and leaves a neutron star or black hole
It collapses into a brown dwarf and stays dim for good
It returns to being a protostar and starts again

items.explain: A Sun-like star's core collapses into a white dwarf and the outer layers are expelled as a planetary nebula; supernovae are for stars of around ten or more solar masses.

items.prompt: A ball of gas condensed from a collapsing cloud has only about 0.05 times the Sun's mass. What is its fate?

options.label: It becomes a main-sequence star like the Sun
It ends as a supernova
It never fuses hydrogen and is a brown dwarf
It grows into a red giant

items.explain: Protostars below roughly 0.08 solar masses never reach temperatures high enough for hydrogen fusion; these are brown dwarfs.

items.prompt: Once fusion starts in a young star, why does it stop collapsing?

options.label: Its outer layers are blown away by the fusion
Its core goes dark once the star has settled
Its gas cools until it cannot be squeezed more
Core energy holds gas pressure up against its weight

items.explain: Fusion leads to hydrostatic equilibrium: energy released by the core maintains a high gas pressure that balances the weight of the star and prevents further collapse.

items.prompt: A star's core runs out of hydrogen, so the fusion that pushed outward from the core stops. What does the core do?

options.label: It expands and cools
It contracts
It stays the same size
It flies apart at once

items.explain: Without the outward radiation pressure from hydrogen fusion to counteract gravity, the core contracts.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which one?

steps.text: Small, cold red dwarfs fuse hydrogen slowly and stay on the main sequence for hundreds of billions of years.
Massive, hot O-type stars leave the main sequence after just a few million years.
So the more massive a star is, the longer it lasts.
The Sun, in between, stays on the main sequence for about 10 billion years.

beats.explain: The pattern runs the other way: the more massive a star, the shorter its life.

paragraphs.heading: A life too slow to watch
paragraphs.text: Stellar evolution is the way a star changes over time. How long that takes depends on the star's mass: from a few million years for the heaviest stars to trillions of years for the lightest, far longer than the universe has existed so far. No one studies it by watching a single star, because most of the changes are too slow to notice even over centuries. Instead, astrophysicists look at many stars caught at different points in their lives, and simulate how stars are built using computer models.

paragraphs.heading: Born in a collapsing cloud
paragraphs.text: Every star forms from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust, often called a nebula or molecular cloud. The process starts when a giant molecular cloud, typically about 100 light-years across, collapses under its own gravity and breaks into ever smaller pieces. In each piece, the falling gas releases energy as heat. As temperature and pressure climb, a piece condenses into a spinning ball of very hot gas called a protostar. The protostar keeps growing by pulling in gas and dust, and becomes a pre-main-sequence star once it reaches its final mass; what happens after that depends on that mass.

paragraphs.heading: Too small to ignite
paragraphs.text: Astronomers compare masses with the Sun's, so 1.0 M_(☉) means one solar mass. Protostars under roughly 0.08 M_(☉) never get hot enough for hydrogen to fuse. These are called brown dwarfs. They shine dimly and slowly fade, cooling gradually over hundreds of millions of years.

paragraphs.heading: The long middle
paragraphs.text: In a heavier protostar the core eventually reaches 10 million kelvin, and hydrogen begins to fuse, first into deuterium and then into helium. Fusion soon sets up a balance: energy from the core keeps the gas pressure high enough to carry the star's weight and stop further collapse. The star has now settled into the main sequence, and fusion will power it for most of its existence. Small, cool red dwarfs fuse hydrogen slowly and can stay there for hundreds of billions of years or more, while massive, hot O-type stars leave after just a few million. A yellow dwarf like the Sun stays about 10 billion years, and the Sun is thought to be roughly halfway through.

paragraphs.heading: Growing into a giant
paragraphs.text: Sooner or later the core runs out of hydrogen and the star starts to move off the main sequence. In stars like the Sun, once the core is mostly helium, hydrogen fusion carries on in a shell around it. The star slowly grows, passing through the subgiant stage until it becomes a red giant. Stars with at least half the Sun's mass can then fuse helium in the core, while heavier stars can fuse heavier elements in a series of nested shells.

paragraphs.heading: How stars end
paragraphs.text: When a star like the Sun has used up its nuclear fuel, the core shrinks into a dense white dwarf and its outer layers are thrown off as a planetary nebula. Stars of about ten or more times the Sun's mass can blow up in a supernova as their iron cores collapse into a neutron star or a black hole. The smallest red dwarfs have not reached their end yet, because the universe is not old enough. Models suggest they will slowly get brighter and hotter before their hydrogen runs out and they become low-mass white dwarfs.
